en: O Lord of Jinas! Even a slight commencement of the praise of your virtues becomes the supreme cause for the destruction of all karmas;
such is my firm resolve, and therefore, with great reverence—
O Sugata! I shall compose a hymn, exquisite through its adherence to the method of the explicit meaning. ||1||
Whether it be mati, śruta, or avadhi, these are indeed your innate means of valid cognition; therefore, you, the Self-existent One, have yourself awakened to the path of liberation.
And this is not something that can be perceived here by those like us, even with divine vision.
Just as all royal splendors and the like belong to those who have performed meritorious deeds. ||2||
You are devoted to vows, you long for incomparable bliss, you fear the cycle of existence, and you loathe the slaughter of living beings;
yet at times, you suddenly arise without compassion, even while being devoid of consciousness.
Nevertheless, you are accepted as the Guru, the Jina who is the sole kinsman of the three worlds. ||3||
Through your accumulated austerity,
there arose for you that supreme knowledge which encompasses all objects, is free from sensory defects, is not subject to rebirth, is self-born,
follows an unobstructed sequence, and is by nature devoid of any admixture with other things.
That alone is accepted by yogins as the essence of the goal of human life. ||4||
O Victor! Your teaching is contradictory, filled with various branches of fallacious arguments, and difficult for ordinary people to navigate;
yet it is accepted by the truly wise—this is not at all surprising.
"For even the harsh words spoken by great souls result in renown. (5)
The vast and priceless lion-throne fashioned by the Lord of the Gods, as well as the threefold protection against the heat, the shimmering fly-whisks,
sovereignty over the three worlds, and incomparable detachment.
These two things are not compatible in you; nevertheless, they coexist.
You speak harshly, intent upon the restraint of the senses; you exhaust those who have taken refuge in asceticism, however difficult and faultless it may be,
with a protection of the six classes of living beings that is observed by no one else.
Oh, even though he is intent on bestowing grace, there is no one else who is the soul of the three worlds! || 7 ||
O Lord! Though You do not take pleasure in those intent on Your praise, You grant them incomparable happiness;
and though not provoked to anger, You surely cast the envious into miserable states of rebirth—yet this does not contradict Your status as the Supreme Being.
He neither becomes angry nor does he rejoice, remaining established in the middle state which is his natural disposition.
For you, whose karma has been completely exhausted, there is never any passion or the like, nor any fluctuations of the senses, nor any mental engagement with objects; and yet,
you simultaneously and effortlessly know the entire world.
And you perceive [all things] with the divine, truly real eye that has arisen in its entirety. ||9||

And through the destruction of those actions that produce passion, attachment, delusion, and fear, there is victory over the enemies that are the afflictions (kaṣāyas), the arising of the knowledge of all reality,
and for you, a bliss unequaled by anything else and sovereignty over the three worlds.
O Lord! This has been firmly established by the tradition of the excellent sages and others. ||10||

For your word is not contradicted by sensory perception, nor by inference, nor even by what is accepted by logic; O Sage of excellent method, it is joined in seven ways and is free from all doubt because no false cause is observed. Therefore, O Blessed One, you alone are the state of the Supreme Lord.
You are not understood to be greedy because of your renunciation of all attachments;
nor is there any delusion in you, since your speech is free from fault;
nor are you hateful, because of your manifold protection of living beings.
Moreover, because you are unarmed, your fear has likewise vanished. ||12||
If even you speak falsely in this way, O Jina, what then can be said of others who, though being authoritative, are by nature greedy, deluded, and so forth? Furthermore,
a collection of words that is not composed by an agent is never observed.
Furthermore, oh! even rebirth is not contradicted by reasonings. ||13||

Because we hear names such as those of the author’s father, mother, death, sage-lineage (*gotra*), and Vedic school (*caraṇa*), and because we observe the restriction of multiple words to specific combinations, and because we hear [the Vedas] as having the nature of being causes for the engagement and withdrawal of persons seeking results—just like the *Manusūtra*—the Śruti is indeed composed by a human author. (14)
Furthermore, the recollection of a previous birth is clearly observed in some individuals here [in this world], whether through the words of a reliable person or from widespread popular tradition.
Moreover, there is no arising of what is non-existent, nor is there the destruction of what is existent without a cause.
For how can one who has no attachment to living beings in the world beyond be called a non-attached person? (15)
Furthermore, that which is non-existent is not produced, nor is that which already exists merely manifested—
as in the case of the various parts of wine or the diverse colors of a peacock’s plumage.
Nor is it observed in certain cases, such as when a pot and other vessels are used for the purpose of cooking dead food.
How can consciousness be accepted as a quality resulting from contact with earth, water, and so forth? (16)

Your body, with its senses stilled and even devoid of ornaments, has become a supreme festival for the hearts and eyes of all people; O Jina, even without taking up weapons, you have conquered those who are difficult to conquer.
The enemies of the astringent [flavor] are not overcome by others, even when they have seized their weapons. ||17||
Through the observation of the consistency in the attainment of the innermost goal by means of wisdom,
there may arise in some cases here a supreme establishment, like the measurement of space;
yet, abandonment is also seen in some cases where that which is subject to decay is uprooted.
In the same way, this destruction of the passions is also logical, like the extinguishing of a fire. ||18||

O Jina! Here, one who knows the general nature of both the existent and the non-existent is seen to be all-knowing; if this is so even for one who is merely human by nature, how much more so for one possessing complete knowledge?
For at some time, in some place, and for someone here, there may exist the state of being free from passion and other defilements.
Is it not clearly perceived, much less by you who are free from sin? ||19||
Your skill in teaching the reality of all things, from the self onwards, without exception—
a hallmark of your unique authority that is unshared by any other person—
is not found in the words spoken by the sages Kaṇāda, Kapila, Akṣapāda, nor by the son of the Śākyas.
For even those with excellent vision and other faculties stumble, even regarding objects determined with certainty. (20)
The Puruṣa is held by others to be unchanging in every respect; otherwise, there would be a total loss of the reality of the objects of valid cognition and so forth.
Furthermore, due to the absence of passions (kaṣāya), he has no bondage by means of karmas.
Furthermore, how could there be final nirvana if things possess a momentary nature? Thus [it is said]. (21)

The mind is subject to transformation; it undergoes the cycle of worldly existence here, and yet it is that very same mind which is liberated. Thus, the conceptualization of a "person" (puruṣa) would be in vain.
Furthermore, no modification of this mind is possible in any way whatsoever.
For it is certain that when one is angry, they will surely resort to speaking both sides of the matter.
The teaching composed by others, which accords with the minds of ordinary worldlings,
holds that happiness is attained through ease and not through austerity for those whose senses are not subdued;
it maintains that all conditioned phenomena are subject to disintegration at every moment.
Is it not the case that this is contradicted by the logical marks (liṅga) ascertained through one's own system and common worldly consensus? ||23||
The continuum is neither eternal nor impermanent, nor is it both;
since it is thus asserted to be a mere non-entity like a forest and so forth in reality,
activities such as farming, giving, moral conduct, and venerating sages would be entirely in vain.
If it were somehow indestructible, there would be a contradiction of the thesis. ||24||
Though you are the Supreme Being beyond all others and have transcended the human state, you are now praised by foolish men as "a mere human.
Where is your nature as a human, and where is your passionless omniscience? For in reality, the condition of being subject to birth and death does not exist in you. (25)
Although your origin here is held to be from your mother’s womb— like a choice lotus petal unsoiled by impurities—
even in the womb you were not one whose heart was devoid of the discernment between the beneficial and the harmful.
How can it be suspected that you are merely like an ordinary human being? ||26||
Even death does not exist for you as it does for an ordinary human; for one who has died, there is final nirvana rather than a rebirth through death.
Furthermore, there is no old age, since your body has arisen from that which is stainless and absolute.
From that point on, until death, it remains in a single form, free from disease.

Others, wretched and like gods, themselves lacking true happiness, pray for a pleasure based on the proximity of another— such as the service of young women; but by you, the Supreme Self, no such pleasure is sought from another, since your bliss is inherent.
Free from transformation, incomparable, eternal, and born of its own self. ||28||
Surrounded by hosts of *piśācas*, Hara dances wildly in the cremation ground, effortlessly wearing the skin of a terrifying elephant dripping with blood;
he laughs loudly with a roar of "kahakahā" and boisterous peals of laughter.
How is he worshipped by the wise as the supreme deity? ||29||
With his broad right mouth, he indeed devours the corpses, putrid marrow, blood, entrails, and flesh of all living beings;
accompanied by hosts similar to himself, he takes intense delight day and night.
Moreover, how can one who drinks liquor be a vessel for trustworthiness? (30)
That which is without beginning or end, which brings about the awakening to all principles,
which possesses sovereignty over the entire world, and furthermore, which is characterized by complete contentment as well as freedom from defects— that indeed is what is called "false."
And because it is devoid of sound reasoning, there is no scripture regarding the perfectly pure reality. ||31||
From the water-pot, deer-skin, rosary, and so forth, one infers that Brahmā is defiled by faults such as a lack of purity;
and from their bearing weapons, fear and cruelty are inferred in Viṣṇu and Hara.
There is no inherent charm, and the state of being utterly deluded is merely a result of ornamentation. //32//
If he creates living beings himself, why does he destroy the Daityas?
If you say it is for the sake of suppressing wicked people, then non-creation would have been better;
for one who has already accomplished what was to be done, the creation of worlds is fruitless.
If it is argued that this is its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), then that [nature] is indeed obtained as something utterly false and corrupted. ||33||
For those whose minds are alternately pleased and provoked, there will inevitably arise suffering as well as delusion, fear, calamity,
and disease; moreover, they will suffer from thirst and hunger, and yet the cycle of existence is not severed.
O Lord of Jinas! How could reliability be appropriate for you in relation to others? ||34||

How is it that those who are themselves afflicted and tormented by the fear of enemies become the cause for the arising of happiness in others, and how do they become a refuge for those who are afraid?
Alas, this is due to people who, following the path of the worldly, have placed their devotion in you rather than in another.
Frequenting improper resorts is accepted as a cause for rebirth in hell. ||35||
For embodied beings whose minds are constantly engaged in consenting to killing, slaughtering, and the like, and who rejoice in those things arising from corrupt conduct,
a bond of evil is inevitably attached to them in reality.
Even in the case of the auspicious, one who is firmly resolved [upon it] may become a cause for the threefold bondage. ||36||
Why indeed were those various activities— consisting of the bliss of liberation, shrines, giving, and worship— which cause suffering and death for embodied beings,
not taught by you who are the blazing Absolute alone?
These were personally performed by the disciples who had extended their devotion toward you. ||37||
O Jina! By you, or by some person following your instruction, the act of making offerings at a *caitya* has been taught in some way;
as well as the rite of fasting unto death (*anāśaka-vidhi*) or the plucking out of the hair (*keśa-pariluñcana*).
It is understood from another means of valid cognition, which consists of [the stages] beginning with hearing and ending with the final realization. ||38||

Furthermore, you do not necessarily hold that what causes suffering to living beings leads invariably to the unwholesome, nor does it lead to the wholesome; for one who speaks the truth is not entirely so in every respect.
Nor, moreover, is self-restraint and generosity exclusively the cause of the wholesome.
Your doctrine is a dense thicket of a web of diverse methods and logical analyses. ||39||
If you too have established this teaching here for the sake of living in comfort, how is it appropriate for you to be a teacher who abandons and rejects everything?
Likewise, by means of such practices as fasting, eating only half a meal, and the avoidance of flavors, you alone have attained the title of "Jina" (Victor) through the mastery of the senses. ||40||

O Lord of Jinas! This practice of yours—taking up robes, garments, and bowls—is not conceived by you as a cause of happiness after due reflection; rather, it was devised by those who were themselves incapable [of the higher path].
Yet, even this may become for you a true path, just like your state of nakedness.
When fruit is easily obtainable by hand, one does not climb the tree. ||41||
For those who possess possessions, fear inevitably arises,
as do anger, violence, harsh speech, and falsehood; furthermore, there is the sense of "mine," the threat of thieves, and the distraction of one's own mind.
For how could those of defiled nature possess the supreme, pure, and true meditative concentration? (42)

When these embodied beings, being exceedingly subtle in nature, look upon the various foods and drinks contained within their own vessels, then, if even a drop were discarded, it would result in their death or else in the suffocation of many others through the resulting commotion. (43)
It is understood that those who abide in nakedness, who always eat only what their own arms provide,
and whose intentions are ever free from negligence— even when committing the slaughter of many living beings—
do not partake in the fruit of bondage.
Even now, these [beings] continue to maintain their activity according to what is suitable for their own strength.

If, for those who abide according to the scriptures, whose minds are intent on effort regarding food, drink, and edibles, and who perceive with unimpaired senses, there should arise some demerit from the slight affliction of living beings, then even asceticism would be mere slaughter for you, because it causes torment to the life-continuum of oneself and others. (45)
In fire, wind, earth, and water, there is always an inherent mutual opposition; thus, the absence of life is logically established in some cases.
However, for those who have committed offenses through negligence, the removal of that fault occurs in certain instances by means of their own sacred tradition (*āgama*).
How can there be fault in those who abide in bliss, dwelling in the sky? 46.

Others, such as Kapila and his followers, have proclaimed the destruction of one's own virtues and the truth, as well as the ruin of the goals of human existence, resulting in a state of non-abundant liberation; yet by you,
whose sins are thoroughly crushed and who possesses the splendor of the blazing flood of pure knowledge, [this has been overturned].
It is certainly eternal, of incomparable nature, infinite, and unimpeded bliss. ||47||
Others maintain that liberation in this world consists in a total, unconditioned cessation;
yet no one who is not a fool exerts himself for his own ruin.
[But you hold that liberation] consists in the attainment of excellence through the integration of favorable qualities.
In your teaching, it is proclaimed that stability consists of Śiva alone. ||48||
Thus, even this praise of virtues becomes a sufficient means for supreme liberation;
therefore, people who are resolute and yearn for that [liberation] cease from the pursuit of gain through the charming greed of the virtuous.
Indeed, the attainment of what the mind desires is surely the very limit of all exertion. ||49||

Thus, O Great-souled Jina, as I incessantly praise with devotion the synthesis of your qualities—which are of immeasurable power—may there be for me, through that great and absolute glory of prosperity, an unblemished, infinite happiness established within my own self. (50)
